Russell Brand to learn sentence after being found guilty of rapeComedian Brand faces a "significant" prison sentence, which a London court judge is set to hand down on Monday.
Russell Brand to learn sentence after being found guilty of rape and sexual assault
Comedian and actor Russell Brand leaves Southwark Crown Court in London, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.Alastair Grant/APhide caption
Comedian Russell Brand faces a "significant" prison sentence, which a London court judge is set to hand down on Monday.
On Thursday the one-time MTV host turned Christian and spiritual influencer was found guilty on three counts of sexual assault and one of rape, after a four-week trial that garnered massive media attention.
Brand had denied all charges and said he never had sex without consent.
From comedian to convicted rapist: What to know about Russell Brand
After the jury handed down the verdict, Judge Joel Bennathan told Brand, 51, that he faced a "significant custodial term."
Danny Shaw, a crime commentator and former BBC correspondent,postedon X that while the maximum sentence for rape in the UK is life, 10 years is the average sentence, and Brand was likely to receive between four to 13 years of prison time.
The trial examined seven historic charges against Brand, brought forward by six different women. He was found guilty on four of the charges: for raping a woman who'd been to one of his comedy shows in 2009, and sexually assaulting three others between 2004 and 2009. The locations of the sexual assaults were a bar, radio station and TV studio. Brand was also found not guilty of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.
Brand's lawyer asked the judge on Thursday to grant his client bail so that he could spend the weekend with his three children, which the judge denied. Instead the one-time celebrity darling spent his first weekend in a prison cell in London.
He showed little emotion when the verdict was handed down, though his wife Laura — who has supported him throughout — quickly left the courtroom.
Many have called the verdict a significant milestone in the #MeToo movement, which has seen influential men held to account for using their power to abuse women.
Brand has also faced allegations of crimes in the United States. In 2023, a woman, named only as "Jane Doe,"accusedBrand of sexually assaulting her while she was working as a film extra during the making of the 2010 comedy movie "Arthur." That year, Brand married pop star Katy Perry, though the union lasted for just over a year before they divorced.
Addressing the media last week, London police detective Andy Furphy said that Brand had "used his influence, status and fame to prey on women — as his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement."
Camilla Long, a journalist forThe Sunday Times— one of the first newspapers that investigated allegations of abuse against Brand —wrotein a column this weekend that "To sit in court 3 at Southwark crown court, hearing how Brand grabbed, pushed, groped and degraded his victims, was one of the most disgusting experiences of my life."
Long questioned how Brand got away with his behavior for so long, saying: "Never has a predator so loudly declared himself, yet been so roundly ignored."

Russell Brand suspected to have attacked at least 10 other women
Met police chief says ‘many more’ victims could come forward, as actor and comedian awaits sentencing
Police are bracing themselves for more victims of Russell Brand to come forward, with at least 10 more women suspected of having been attacked by the disgraced star.
Brand, 51, will be sentenced on Monday to what is expected to be a lengthy jail sentence for rape and sexual assaults after he abused his fame to become a “predator” targeting women, and got away with it for years.
The fallout from Brand’s case saw the government pledge to examine calls to crack down on “rape myths” in trials.
The Guardian also understands that next week the Metropolitan police team that built the case against Brand will start sifting through reports and intelligence about other potential victims.
The Met commissioner, Sir Mark Rowley, said there could be “many more” victims, but declined to say how many, with some intelligence about further victims being third-hand and some further suspected victims reluctant to face the criminal justice system.
Sources say it is feared the number of further victims is at least in “double digits”, with 10 currently seen as a minimum.
The Met police said on Thursday that Brand was under investigation for two further rape allegations. Detectives have sent files to specialist rape prosecutors and are in discussions with them over the material.
Rowley said: “We’ve got two other victims who’ve come forward who want to tell their story, and so two rape cases we’re investigating. I wouldn’t be surprised if many, many more come forward, and we’re open to that.”
Rowley declined on LBC Radio to confirm the new allegations would reach “double figures”, and said: “I’m not going to guess on this, but we’ve seen in the past with high-profile individuals who are brought to justice that it does often bring out a flood of other cases. Let’s see where this one goes.”
Brand’s trial, which spanned claims of attacks from 1999 to 2009, saw women asked by the defence barrister why they had not screamed during attacks.
Since the end of the trial there has been a debate about rape myths. A No 10 source said the prime minister, Andy Burnham, believed calls from the victims’ commissioner, Claire Waxman, for a legal duty that would require judges to issue directions to juries on rape myths and misconceptions, should be examined.
A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said:“Rape myths have absolutely no place in our courts and victims should never feel as though they are the ones on trial.
“Judges are already able to give directions to counter rape myths … we will also carefully consider the victims’ commissioner’s proposals as we continue to strengthen protections for victims.”
Siobhan Blake, the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) lead for rape and serious sexual offences, said: “The focus must be the actions of the perpetrator and not the behaviour of the victim.
“We know that there is no typical response to sexual assault and myths that victims should scream and fight back are outdated. Some people may freeze or feel unable to speak about it for months or even years, but this is not a barrier to justice.”
Brand now faces years of imprisonment and the growing prospect of a fresh trial over further allegations.
He was convicted on Thursday of raping a young fan at his luxury London townhouse in 2009, continuing despite her pleas for him to stop. He had picked her out of a crowd. He was also found guilty of sexually assaulting three women in separate incidents at a radio station, a recording studio and a bar.
Victims are expected to tell of the impact his crimes had on them in court on Monday.
Brand became an international star, acting in Hollywood films, and in latter years an online influencer, but was dogged by whispers and allegations about his danger to women. He was accused of treating women as a “disposable commodity” and a “means to an end” to satisfy his voracious sexual appetite.
The government says it is committed to reducing violence against women and girls by half.
Burnham told Times Radio: “It’s horrifying what Russell Brand has done. And I’d firstly like to praise the bravery of the women, the victims in the case, who’ve come forward and had the courage to speak out.
“But yes, the journalists too, who supported those who had been abused by Russell Brand. So all of them deserve our praise for having that courage to come forward.”
Later on the BBC, Burnham was asked about a statement of support for Brand in 2014 as the star faced media criticism, and said: “Well, over a decade ago, and all I can say is I had no idea of the full extent of what he was doing or what he went on to do. His crimes are horrific.”
Burnham told Times Radio he will look at making changes to rape trials so that they “do not leave the woman feeling like she is on trial”.
He said: “We need to constantly look at the way rape trials are conducted to make sure that they do not leave the woman feeling like she is on trial in court, as has been the experience of people in the past … we need to encourage more women to come forward to report rape.”
The comedian Katherine Ryan, who warned of a “predator” in the entertainment industry before Brand’s trial, said she felt relief at his conviction.
“They came forward despite Russell Brand having fame, power, money and a legion of fans ready to attack them,” she said.
“I will never be someone who, like, dances on graves. There has been some justice done today. There’s a level of relief, but there’s grief alongside relief.”
Bear Grylls, who baptised Brand when he converted to Christianity in 2024, said the star’s faith seemed genuine and added: “It is right that justice has now been served. I can’t imagine how hard this time has been for the victims, the heroes of the day.”
Brand was cleared of two further charges of rape and one allegation of attempted indecent assault.
Brand’s victims told how he “snapped” – changing from charming to nasty – as he raped and sexually assaulted them before gaslighting them into believing nothing was wrong.

Katherine Ryan says she feels 'grief and relief' after Russell Brand conviction - BBC News
Listen: Katherine Ryan speaks about Brand guilty verdict
ByHelena Wilkinson & Paul GlynnBBC News
Comedian Katherine Ryan has said she feels "grief and relief" after Russell Brand was convicted of rape and sexual assault.
The Canadian stand-up and TV star said there were "a lot of women speaking privately and quietly" following Thursday's verdict, who feel "a very nuanced mix of emotions".
Ryan had previously claimed in a BBC TV documentaryinterview with Louis Therouxthat there was a "predator" in the entertainment industry.
Ryan said in 2022 that she could not name the famous man as it would be a "litigious minefield" but mentioned that she had appeared on a TV programme with him and told him he was a "predator" to "his face".
It was widely rumoured Ryan had been referring to her time on Comedy Central's Roast Battle in 2018 alongside Brand, but she has not confirmed she was referring to him, and she did not name the show she was working on.
Speaking about the guilty verdict of his trial, on the latest episode of her podcast Telling Everybody Everything, Ryan said: "It really made me feel just quite dysregulated again, caught off-guard, emotional, in awe of the survivors who also had nothing to gain.
"They came forward despite Russell Brand having fame, power, money, and a legion of fans ready to attack them."
She added: "I will never be someone who like, dances on graves. There has been some justice done today. There's a level of relief, but there's grief alongside relief.
"Everything's nuanced, and it was proved in court that a terrible thing happened, and that means that a terrible thing happened.
"I just think again and again about people who have been hurt, and who have to carry that, who've carried that around long enough, and will continue to carry that in some way, regardless of what justice is done."
Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault
Brand was found guilty on Thursday of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.
The former entertainer was acquitted of two other rape charges and one allegation of attempted indecent assault.
The 51-year-old will be sentenced on Monday. The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, told him to expect "a significant custodial term" after the verdicts were delivered.
Ryan continued on the podcast: "This verdict came because women were hurt, and I worry as well about what happens next.
"Because he's obviously spent a long time cultivating this idea that the establishment have invented these claims against him, and he's martyred himself to a growing audience who really still think that it is the courageous survivors who are the villains in this story."
Ryan's comments came on the same day that former BBC One controller Lorraine Heggessey questioned how and why Brand was able to "get away with it so long?
"Why didn't anybody intervene? Why did those around him enable him? Why didn't any of the senior executives who worked with him call time?" she said on BBC Radio 5 Live's Nick Campbell on Friday.
"I think they were partly mesmerised. I think he seemed to be 'cool' for a while. I think he did have charisma," added Heggessey.
"He brought in a young audience, which a lot of broadcasters crave. So I think all of those reasons... and as people have said, he did hide in plain sight."
'Justice is served' says Bear Grylls
Bear Grylls, the adventurer and host of the Discovery Channel's show Man Vs Wild, has spoken about when he helped baptise Brand in the River Thames in 2024.
"Brand's faith seemed genuine to me at the time when I was a guest at his private baptism," he said on X, adding that he had attended a few baptisms, including "visiting in prisons with people who have committed terrible crimes".
Grylls said he attended as part of a calling of his faith "to love and serve anyone", adding it is "the sick who need healing".
"Judgement is for the courts and God… I wouldn't want to ever discourage someone's coming to faith," he continued.
But, he said, it was “right that justice has now been served.
"I can't imagine how hard this time has been for the victims, the heroes of the day."
Brand is now also being investigated over further rape allegations made by two women, police have now said.
Details in legal documents from a hearing at London's Southwark Crown Court before Brand's criminal trial began suggest that one of the women was 16 years old at the time and featured in a Channel 4 documentary.
Brand was accused by four women of rape, sexual assaults and emotional abuse in a joint Channel 4 Dispatches, Times and Sunday Times investigation in September 2023.
The actor and comedian denied the allegations.
None of the women who featured in the media investigation were the complainants from Brand's criminal trial.
On Thursday it emerged that Brand was facing further rape allegations made by two women. The Metropolitan police said he had previously been interviewed under caution in relation to them.
During a pre-trial hearing in October Brand tried unsuccessfully to have his criminal case thrown out.
His lawyers argued that the actor and entertainer couldn't receive a fair trial because of the publicity following the Dispatches programme.
Prosecutors opposed Brand's application to have his case stopped.
It was during that hearing that the prosecution said one of the complaints made in the documentary was being investigated.
Riel Karmy-Jones KC said: "Of the four women in the Ch4 documentary, two concern events outside the jurisdiction.
"One did not disclose any offence. The other is being investigated.
"There had been some interaction in 2018, she did not report the matter until 2024, after the documentary was aired."
In documents submitted to the court for the hearing prosecutors also said it was "plainly incorrect" to say there had been a decision not to investigate.
"The outstanding charges against RB in respect of 'Alice' from Dispatches demonstrate that there has been no such decision – rather that the police will and have responded appropriately once a formal allegation is made."
The head of the Metropolitan Police has said he "wouldn't be surprised" if more people came forward to make allegations about Russell Brand.
Sir Mark Rowley also told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday that what he heard reported from Brand's trial at Southwark Crown Court came very close to "victim blaming".

fact_units.text: Russell Brand to learn sentence after being found guilty of rape : NPRAccessibility links
Russell Brand to learn sentence after being found guilty of rapeComedian Brand faces a "significant" prison sentence, which a London court judge is set to hand down on Monday.
Russell Brand to learn sentence after being found guilty of rape and sexual assault
Comedian and actor Russell Brand leaves Southwark Crown Court in London, Tuesday, Nov.
Comedian Russell Brand faces a "significant" prison sentence, which a London court judge is set to hand down on Monday.

On Thursday the one-time MTV host turned Christian and spiritual influencer was found guilty on three counts of sexual assault and one of rape, after a four-week trial that garnered massive media attention.
Brand had denied all charges and said he never had sex without consent.
From comedian to convicted rapist: What to know about Russell Brand
After the jury handed down the verdict, Judge Joel Bennathan told Brand, 51, that he faced a "significant custodial term."

Danny Shaw, a crime commentator and former BBC correspondent,postedon X that while the maximum sentence for rape in the UK is life, 10 years is the average sentence, and Brand was likely to receive between four to 13 years of prison time.
The trial examined seven historic charges against Brand, brought forward by six different women.
He was found guilty on four of the charges: for raping a woman who'd been to one of his comedy shows in 2009, and sexually assaulting three others between 2004 and 2009.
The locations of the sexual assaults were a bar, radio station and TV studio.
Brand was also found not guilty of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.
Brand's lawyer asked the judge on Thursday to grant his client bail so that he could spend the weekend with his three children, which the judge denied.
Instead the one-time celebrity darling spent his first weekend in a prison cell in London.
He showed little emotion when the verdict was handed down, though his wife Laura — who has supported him throughout — quickly left the courtroom.
Many have called the verdict a significant milestone in the #MeToo movement, which has seen influential men held to account for using their power to abuse women.
Brand has also faced allegations of crimes in the United States.

In 2023, a woman, named only as "Jane Doe,"accusedBrand of sexually assaulting her while she was working as a film extra during the making of the 2010 comedy movie "Arthur." That year, Brand married pop star Katy Perry, though the union lasted for just over a year before they divorced.

Addressing the media last week, London police detective Andy Furphy said that Brand had "used his influence, status and fame to prey on women — as his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement."

Camilla Long, a journalist forThe Sunday Times— one of the first newspapers that investigated allegations of abuse against Brand —wrotein a column this weekend that "To sit in court 3 at Southwark crown court, hearing how Brand grabbed, pushed, groped and degraded his victims, was one of the most disgusting experiences of my life."
Long questioned how Brand got away with his behavior for so long, saying: "Never has a predator so loudly declared himself, yet been so roundly ignored."

Russell Brand faces the growing prospect of a fresh trial over further allegations.Photograph: Kin Cheung/APView image in fullscreenRussell Brand faces the growing prospect of a fresh trial over further allegations.Photograph: Kin Cheung/AP
Russell Brand suspected to have attacked at least 10 other women
Met police chief says ‘many more’ victims could come forward, as actor and comedian awaits sentencing
Police are bracing themselves for more victims of Russell Brand to come forward, with at least 10 more women suspected of having been attacked by the disgraced star.

Brand, 51, will be sentenced on Monday to what is expected to be a lengthy jail sentence for rape and sexual assaults after he abused his fame to become a “predator” targeting women, and got away with it for years.
The fallout from Brand’s case saw the government pledge to examine calls to crack down on “rape myths” in trials.
The Guardian also understands that next week the Metropolitan police team that built the case against Brand will start sifting through reports and intelligence about other potential victims.

The Met commissioner, Sir Mark Rowley, said there could be “many more” victims, but declined to say how many, with some intelligence about further victims being third-hand and some further suspected victims reluctant to face the criminal justice system.
Sources say it is feared the number of further victims is at least in “double digits”, with 10 currently seen as a minimum.
The Met police said on Thursday that Brand was under investigation for two further rape allegations.
Detectives have sent files to specialist rape prosecutors and are in discussions with them over the material.
Rowley said: “We’ve got two other victims who’ve come forward who want to tell their story, and so two rape cases we’re investigating.
I wouldn’t be surprised if many, many more come forward, and we’re open to that.”

Rowley declined on LBC Radio to confirm the new allegations would reach “double figures”, and said: “I’m not going to guess on this, but we’ve seen in the past with high-profile individuals who are brought to justice that it does often bring out a flood of other cases.

article.title: Xứ Wales thắng nhọc Nhật Bản tại Nations Championship: Còn nhiều việc phải làm
article.summary: Dù giành chiến thắng 28-21 trước Nhật Bản trong khuôn khổ Nations Championship, đội tuyển bóng bầu dục Xứ Wales vẫn để lại nhiều lo lắng khi thể hiện một phong độ thiếu thuyết phục.
body: Đội tuyển bóng bầu dục Xứ Wales đã có khởi đầu chiến dịch Nations Championship bằng chiến thắng 28-21 trước Nhật Bản tại Sân vận động Principality. Dù giành được kết quả có lợi cùng điểm thưởng, màn trình diễn của đội chủ nhà lại vấp phải nhiều hoài nghi từ giới chuyên môn lẫn ban huấn luyện do sự thiếu sắc bén và thế trận chật vật trước đối thủ.

Phát biểu sau trận đấu, huấn luyện viên trưởng Steve Tandy thừa nhận đội bóng chơi dưới kỳ vọng và thiếu đi sự quyết đoán cần thiết. Trong khi đó, đội trưởng Dewi Lake cũng thẳng thắn chia sẻ rằng tập thể Xứ Wales đã có những thời điểm tự làm khó mình. Điểm sáng lớn nhất trong đội hình chủ nhà là cầu thủ chạy cánh Louis Rees-Zammit, người đã tỏa sáng rực rỡ để mang về giải thưởng cầu thủ xuất sắc nhất trận sau thời gian ngắn thử sức với bóng bầu dục Mỹ.

Dù vậy, những thống kê chuyên môn cho thấy Xứ Wales gặp nhiều khó khăn khi chỉ kiểm soát 40% thời gian cầm bóng và phải thực hiện đến 227 pha cản phá so với 115 của Nhật Bản. Hàng ranh biên (line-out) của đội chủ nhà cũng gặp trục trặc nghiêm trọng với sáu lần ném hỏng, tạo điều kiện cho các cầu thủ Nhật Bản duy trì áp lực cho đến những phút cuối cùng.

Thử thách sắp tới của Xứ Wales sẽ nặng đô hơn rất nhiều khi họ chuẩn bị đón tiếp New Zealand và Australia trên sân nhà trong các tuần tiếp theo. Với những hạn chế bộc lộ trong trận gặp Nhật Bản, ban huấn luyện hiểu rõ đội bóng cần phải nhanh chóng khắc phục các điểm yếu nếu không muốn trả giá đắt trước các đối thủ hàng đầu thế giới.

Who is Anthony Joshua's trainer? Why heavyweight made yet another change in advance of Tyson Fury fight | Sporting NewsSkip to main content
Who is Anthony Joshua's trainer? Why heavyweight made yet another change in advance of Tyson Fury fight
For a fighter who is, largely unfairly, criticised for having a gilded existence in boxing, Anthony Joshua always seems to be searching.
The British star entered professional boxing as a 2012 Olympic gold medalist, won a world title in his 16th fight and is a former two-time unified heavyweight champion.
But for the past seven years, Joshua has made frequent changes to his training setup, employing several esteemed boxing minds to serve as his chief second.
"Every coach has added something unique," he told The Sporting News earlier this year. "But where I'm at now, the coaches have just got to trust me as well because I've been around the block. I have to streamline all that stuff that I've learned, and have a relationship with the coach where the coach also has to understand that he can be taught as well."
He added: "What I've learned in my career is to try and work with specialists. If you want to be the best, there's specialists in every field. There's people who know what they're doing and know what they're talking about; there's also people that blag what they're doing and blag what they're talking about. And there's also specialists who are the creme de la creme."
Ahead of his huge and long-awaited showdown with Tyson Fury in Cardiff this Saturday, Joshua once again tweaked his training setup.
MORE:Fury and Joshua are best of enemies in friendly London launch
Ben Davisonwill run Joshua's corner, beginning a second spell as the 37-year-old's lead trainer.
Davison famously oversaw Fury’s journey from drug and alcohol abuse, depression and obesity back to the heavyweight elite. Their five bouts together included Fury's dramatic draw against Deontay Wilder in their initial fight.
The Essex-based trainer worked with former two-weight world champion Billy Joe Saunders around that time and helmed Josh Taylor's successful bid to become undisputed super lightweight champion against Jose Ramirez in May 2021. Leigh Wood's against-the-odds run to twice reign as WBA featherweight champion perhaps represents Davison's best work. He also came in to help steer Fabio Wardley's unique journey from white-collar novice to heavyweight world champion. American pound-for-pound star Devin Haney also works with Davison and his chief video analyst, Lee Wylie, on a consultancy basis.
Rising British featherweight prospect Shabaz Masoud and recent heavyweight title challenger Moses Itauma are star pupils at the Ben Davison Performance Centre, where assistant coach Barry Smith is also a key part of the setup.
MORE:An in-depth look at Ben Davison's training methods
Davison's focus on drilling and video analysis, with Wylie a key part of his setup, has come under scrutiny from proponents of boxing's "old school". But the roll call of high-calibre boxers who continue to work with him despite high-profile recent setbacks speaks volumes. Those fighters are not with Davison as some sort of charity case.
"The whole point of the way we do things is you get a plan, you study it, you drill the scenarios. So by the time you get in there, you haven’t got to overthink it," Davison explained in a 2023 interview with The Sporting News ahead of Wood's dramatic KO win over domestic rival Josh Warrington.
"If you’ve done the work beforehand, when you get in there it becomes instinct rather than having to think in the moment. People might say, ‘Oh, you’re over-complicating by doing things like that…’, you actually don’t. You’re actually doing the complete opposite.
"By trying to work it out in the moment, how many different variables are there that might happen? That is a lot harder — processing what might happen, what he’s going to do, what he’s setting up, etcetera — than to have been through a scouting report, watched plenty of film on the opponent and to have come up with a conclusion that the majority of the time when he does this, you’re looking for that, the majority of the time when you do this, his reaction is going to be that.
"And you drill that to a point where you haven’t got to think about it. It becomes second nature."
Most of the recent criticism of Davison has centred on his in-fight work when the best-laid plans have gone awry – most notably when Itauma spectacularly ran out of gas during his IBF title fight against Filip Hrgovic, having dominated pretty much every round, and during Wardley's punishing back-to-back losses to Dubois. It should be noted that both Itauma and Wardley remained with Davison despite their setbacks, and Joshua must be convinced that Davison's poor run of heavyweight form will turn around on November 11.
Anthony Joshua trainer history: How many coaches has AJ had in boxing career?
Davison was the fifth of six men to have operated as Joshua's chief second across 34 professional fights. But there's a little more to it than that.
The man who helmed the majority of Joshua's career as both an amateur and a professional. McCracken, who trained former two-time super middleweight world champion and current outspoken Joshua sceptic Carl Froch, is the performance director at GB Boxing.
His role at the head of the UK's decorated amateur setup meant he guided Joshua to Olympic gold in 2012. The pair continued to work together when the new national hero turned professional.
Joshua still did plenty of his training with the GB squad at the English Institute of Sport in Sheffield, but McCracken's job with the national setup prevented him from running Joshua's corner on fight nights. That task fell to experienced trainer Tony Sims, most recently noted for his impressive work with Conor Benn.
Sims was in Joshua's corner for his first 17 professional fights, including his IBF world title win over Charles Martin. For his second defence against American Eric Molina in December 2016, McCracken assumed control of the corner on fight night after reaching an agreement with Team GB.
He was a calming and measured voice as Joshua came through the first knockdown of his career to thrillingly defeat veteran former champion Wladimir Klitschko at Wembley in 2017. That began a run of headline stadium fights against Carlos Takam, WBO champion Joseph Parker and Alexander Povetkin, all won and all overseen by McCracken.

Joshua Buatsi and Willy Hutchinson renew their rivalry for the vacant WBC world light-heavyweight title in Manchester on Saturday.
The British rivals first met in a highly entertaining, hard-fought contest on the undercard of Daniel Dubois' win over Anthony Joshua in September 2024.

Scotland's Hutchinson, 28, suffered the second defeat of his professional career that night but two wins since have put him in a position to fight for a first world title.
Can Buatsi repeat his victory? Or will Hutchinson gain revenge in Manchester?
BBC Sport spoke to figures from across the boxing world to get their predictions.

"Hutchinson is a man in form and looks like a man who is matured both physically and mentally. This is a fantastic rematch with the WBC light-heavyweight title on the line. It promises to be an action-packed contest and the pot of gold is massive."
"A rematch that I didn't think would come around but it all makes sense with the added incentive of gold. Someone will leave as world champion. The first time they fought, it was 80-20 Buatsi for me, but Hutchinson was a lot better than I expected.
"He has now closed that gap drastically and now it's 55-45 Buatsi. How much has Callum Smith taken out of Buatsi? On the flip side, Hutchinson, after that defeat, has gone from strength to strength.

Deontay Wilder poses for a photo at York Hall ahead of his April fight with Derek Chisora in London.Photograph: Richard Pelham/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDeontay Wilder poses for a photo at York Hall ahead of his April fight with Derek Chisora in London.Photograph: Richard Pelham/Getty Images
Deontay Wilder to face unbeaten Opetaia on Fury v Joshua undercard in Cardiff
Wilder, 41, has won 43 of his 45 victories by knockout
Australian cruiserweight champion moves up in weight
Cardiff showdown will stream worldwide on Netflix
Deontay Wilder, the former World Boxing Council heavyweight champion, will face unbeaten Australian cruiserweight world champion Jai Opetaia on the undercard of Tyson Fury’s showdown with Anthony Joshua in Cardiff on 11 December, organizersannouncedon Wednesday.
Opetaia will move up to heavyweight to take onone of history’s most devastating punchersat the Principality Stadium with the event streaming live worldwide on Netflix.
Accidental champion Deontay Wilder was the American dream misunderstood | Bryan Armen GrahamRead more
Wilder, 41, held the WBC’s version of the heavyweight title from 2015 to 2020, making 10 successful defenses beforelosing his belt to Fury. The American has a professional ledger of 45 wins, four defeats and one draw, with 43 victories coming by knockout.
The 2008 Olympic bronze medalistfrom Tuscaloosa, Alabama,appeared bound for retirementafter aone-sided defeat to Joseph Parkerfollowed by abrutal knockout loss to Zhilei Zhangin 2024, but has since breathed extended life into his career with wins over journeyman Tyrrell Anthony Herndon and two-time world title challenger Derek Chisora.
Opetaia, 31, is unbeaten in 31 professional outings and has established himself as the sport’s leading cruiserweight. The Australian southpaw captured the IBF world title with a victory over Mairis Briedis in 2022 and has since dominated all comers in the 200lb division.
A former Olympian who represented Australia at the 2012 London Games aged 16, the Sydneysider will be making his heavyweight debut against Wilder, who stands 6ft 7in and has spent his entire professional career in the division.
The matchup adds another high-profile contest to a card headlined by Fury and Joshua, whoselong-awaited meeting was confirmed in Septemberafter years of unsuccessful negotiations.
View image in fullscreenDeontay Wilder (right) lands a punch on Derek Chisora during their April fight at the O2 Arena in London.Photograph: Richard Pelham/Getty Images
“The co-main event is officially set,” Zuffa Boxing’s Dana White, whosedisputed role in the promotionremains uncertain,said on social media. “These two guys have a combined 67 knockouts. You do not want to miss this fight.”
Is Fury v Joshua about meritocratic sporting excellence or just algorithmic celebrity power? | Jonathan LiewRead more
The undercard for Fury v Wilder will take place on a Friday night, with the main-event ringwalks at the Principality Stadium expected in the small hours of Saturday morning – widely reported to be around 2am.
That is to accommodate a prime-time American audience forNetflix, which will broadcast it globally after its preferred plan to stage the fight at New York’s Madison Square Garden was scuppered.
Both men are attempting to return to the summit of boxing’s prestige division after suffering two defeats apiece against Oleksandr Usyk, the unbeaten former undisputed heavyweight champion from Ukraine whorelinquished his remaining world title beltsin June but insists he has not retired. Fury has won twice since returning to the ring, while Joshua has spent the year rebuilding afterhis knockout loss to Daniel Duboisin 2024.
The rivals came closest to meeting for the undisputed championship in 2021, but the fight collapsed aftera US arbitrator ruledFury was contractually obligatedto face Wilder for a third time.
Joshua subsequentlylost his titles to Usyk, with several attempts to revive the Fury contest falling apart in the years since.

Deontay Wilder will fight Jai Opetaia on the undercard of Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff on December 11.
Unbeaten cruiserweight star Opetaia is stepping up to heavyweight for the first time to box Wilder, a former world champion and renowned as one of the hardest punchers ever in the sport.
In the main event, Fury and Joshua meet in a long-awaited all-British heavyweight fight.
It would be a first high-level heavyweight fight for Opetaia, a previous holder of the IBF championship who has been a force at cruiserweight.

Speaking of Opetaia, Dana White, the Australian's promoter, previously toldSky Sports: "It's a very dangerous fight for him considering where he sits in his division right now.
"But he's a fighter; he'll fight anybody, even at heavyweight with a guy who hits as hard as Wilder does."
Opetaia would likelyreturn to cruiserweightafterwards. He and David Benavidez are considered the two best fighters in the 200lb weight class and Benavidez remains Opetaia's ultimate target.
Jai Opetaia landed a powerful flurry of shots in the ninth round to force a stoppage victory over Noel Mikaelian and accepted the challenge of David Benavidez next. Fight footage courtesy of DAZN.
"That's the fight he really wants. He wants that fight so we've got to figure that one out," White said, adding: "He wants to stay active, he wants to fight and he doesn't care if it's at heavyweight or wherever, he's ready to go."

fact_units.text: Why heavyweight made yet another change in advance of Tyson Fury fight | Sporting NewsSkip to main content
Why heavyweight made yet another change in advance of Tyson Fury fight
For a fighter who is, largely unfairly, criticised for having a gilded existence in boxing, Anthony Joshua always seems to be searching.
The British star entered professional boxing as a 2012 Olympic gold medalist, won a world title in his 16th fight and is a former two-time unified heavyweight champion.
But for the past seven years, Joshua has made frequent changes to his training setup, employing several esteemed boxing minds to serve as his chief second.
"Every coach has added something unique," he told The Sporting News earlier this year.
"But where I'm at now, the coaches have just got to trust me as well because I've been around the block.
I have to streamline all that stuff that I've learned, and have a relationship with the coach where the coach also has to understand that he can be taught as well."
He added: "What I've learned in my career is to try and work with specialists.
If you want to be the best, there's specialists in every field.
There's people who know what they're doing and know what they're talking about; there's also people that blag what they're doing and blag what they're talking about.
And there's also specialists who are the creme de la creme."
Ahead of his huge and long-awaited showdown with Tyson Fury in Cardiff this Saturday, Joshua once again tweaked his training setup.
MORE:Fury and Joshua are best of enemies in friendly London launch
Ben Davisonwill run Joshua's corner, beginning a second spell as the 37-year-old's lead trainer.
Davison famously oversaw Fury’s journey from drug and alcohol abuse, depression and obesity back to the heavyweight elite.
Their five bouts together included Fury's dramatic draw against Deontay Wilder in their initial fight.

The Essex-based trainer worked with former two-weight world champion Billy Joe Saunders around that time and helmed Josh Taylor's successful bid to become undisputed super lightweight champion against Jose Ramirez in May 2021.
Leigh Wood's against-the-odds run to twice reign as WBA featherweight champion perhaps represents Davison's best work.
He also came in to help steer Fabio Wardley's unique journey from white-collar novice to heavyweight world champion.
American pound-for-pound star Devin Haney also works with Davison and his chief video analyst, Lee Wylie, on a consultancy basis.

Rising British featherweight prospect Shabaz Masoud and recent heavyweight title challenger Moses Itauma are star pupils at the Ben Davison Performance Centre, where assistant coach Barry Smith is also a key part of the setup.
Davison's focus on drilling and video analysis, with Wylie a key part of his setup, has come under scrutiny from proponents of boxing's "old school".
But the roll call of high-calibre boxers who continue to work with him despite high-profile recent setbacks speaks volumes.
Those fighters are not with Davison as some sort of charity case.
"The whole point of the way we do things is you get a plan, you study it, you drill the scenarios.
So by the time you get in there, you haven’t got to overthink it," Davison explained in a 2023 interview with The Sporting News ahead of Wood's dramatic KO win over domestic rival Josh Warrington.
"If you’ve done the work beforehand, when you get in there it becomes instinct rather than having to think in the moment.
People might say, ‘Oh, you’re over-complicating by doing things like that…’, you actually don’t.
"By trying to work it out in the moment, how many different variables are there that might happen?

That is a lot harder — processing what might happen, what he’s going to do, what he’s setting up, etcetera — than to have been through a scouting report, watched plenty of film on the opponent and to have come up with a conclusion that the majority of the time when he does this, you’re looking for that, the majority of the time when you do this, his reaction is going to be that.
"And you drill that to a point where you haven’t got to think about it.

Most of the recent criticism of Davison has centred on his in-fight work when the best-laid plans have gone awry – most notably when Itauma spectacularly ran out of gas during his IBF title fight against Filip Hrgovic, having dominated pretty much every round, and during Wardley's punishing back-to-back losses to Dubois.
It should be noted that both Itauma and Wardley remained with Davison despite their setbacks, and Joshua must be convinced that Davison's poor run of heavyweight form will turn around on November 11.
Anthony Joshua trainer history: How many coaches has AJ had in boxing career?
Davison was the fifth of six men to have operated as Joshua's chief second across 34 professional fights.
But there's a little more to it than that.
The man who helmed the majority of Joshua's career as both an amateur and a professional.
McCracken, who trained former two-time super middleweight world champion and current outspoken Joshua sceptic Carl Froch, is the performance director at GB Boxing.
His role at the head of the UK's decorated amateur setup meant he guided Joshua to Olympic gold in 2012.

World Models Will Soon Be Inescapable. Here’s What You Need to Know | WIREDSkip to main content
It’s 2016, andyou’re wandering around the neighborhood at dusk. On the prowl, you’re swiping on a smartphone to catch that elusive Snorlax and grow your collection inPokémon Go. You, alongside hundreds of millions of other players, are enjoying a mixed-reality game built around lovable characters. What you don’t realize is that these scans of your environment will one day helprobotsnavigate obstacles and interact with objects.
Niantic, the creator ofPokémon Go, sold the game last year and pivoted hard into one of Silicon Valley’s buzziest AI topics right now: world models. “We’re very much about reconstructing the real world,” says Brian McClendon,Niantic Spatial’schief technology officer. He hopes to leverage its trove of world data to build replicas. Unlike the text-based nature oflarge language models, world models use visual inputs and can generate digital environments that simulate physics.
Thissoftwareis poised to seep into everyday life, without you necessarily ever interacting directly with world models. 2027 could be a major year for the expansion of home robotics anddriverless cars, both of which are bolstered by advances in world models. It’s time to better understand how these bots think.
“So with a language model, you have a sentence, and it will predict the next word in the sentence,” says Oliver Cameron, the CEO ofOdyssey, an AI lab focused on world models. “With a world model, you give it a visual state of the world, an image, and it will then predict the next visual state of the world.” These 3D generations can be used as digital training grounds. “They’re simulations, but they look and feel real,” he says.
McClendon sees these world models as helping robots practice without physical movement or being in intended environments. He says someone could take photos of where the robot is intended to function, generate a 3D model, and then let the software run “millions of simulations” to train the robot on the space’s parameters.
It’s not justhumanoid robotsthat could use simulated practice; driverless cars also improve using world models. Without a human behind the wheel, split-second software reactions are paramount.
“Importantly, a world model must be able to react to the actions that we take in the world, and so it must understand physics, cause and effect, and how other objects and people change their actions in response to our own,” says Jamie Shotton, chief scientist atWayve, which builds world models designed for cars.
Wayve’s generative world model is powered, in part, by dashcam footage. The startup uses it to recreate hazardous roads and other unsafe conditions that would not be practical to test in real life.
Beyond physical applications, developers are also analyzing how world models could impact video games. Since physics and 3D rendering are core to video games, major players likeTencentare investing in their own world models.
You can expect large AI companies, like Google, to keep boasting about their latest world-model improvements. Investors are also throwing money at insurgent big names in computer science that are turning their attention to the technology.Yann LeCun, Meta’s former chief AI scientist, raisedover a billion dollarsrecently to fund his Advanced Machines Intelligence startup. Additionally, famed Stanfordcomputer scientist Fei-Fei Lilaunched a startup in 2024 calledWorld Labs, whichAMDacquired this year for over $8 billion.
Even if you plan on avoiding autonomous cars and domestic bots altogether, world models are already warping the labor market behind the scenes. To simulate our physical world, AI labs need real people to record it. Earlier this year, I strapped aniPhone to my foreheadand recorded hours of videos in my apartment. I recorded my hands folding laundry, washing dishes, and pouring Diet Coke, selling the video data through an app for a fairly measly payout. As more companies attempt to build better world models, even more gig work may demand this kind of data collection.
Between chasing virtual monsters in 2016 and selling videos of my chores in 2026, these systems are ingesting more and more of my physical life. Now I can’t stop picturing the digital ghost of some humanoid robot trapped inside a simulation of my bedroom, endlessly folding my boxers with its metallic claws—getting slightly better with every pass. I’m sorry I didn’t tidy up first.

Samsung One UI 9.5 Beta May Be Coming Soon: Here's How To Sign Up For The Program
Samsung One UI 9.5 beta may be coming soon: Here's how to sign up for the program
Beta firmware for the Galaxy S26 Ultra is already on Samsung's servers.
ByLuke JamesNov. 7, 2026 8:00 pm ESTdaily_creativity/ShutterstockAdd Engadget on Google:Preferred SourceGoogle Discover
If you've been aggressively refreshing the Samsung Members app on your Galaxy S26 in the hope of seeing the One UI 9.5 beta, you're wasting your time — although you won't have to wait much longer. A One UI 9.5 beta build for theGalaxy S26 Ultrahas appeared on Samsung's Korean and US update servers, which is typically the last step before the company opens registrations.
Samsung hasn't announced the beta or a launch date, but its last point-five update, One UI 8.5, opened to testers on December 8 2025. One UI 9.5 is expected to launch with the Galaxy S27 early in 2027, so a beta release is definitely imminent. If you're interested, signing up will work the same way as last time: register in Samsung Members, then download the beta from your phone's settings once it's available. That is, provided you live in one of six countries — Germany, India, Poland, South Korea, the UK or the US — and own the right phone.
The build that's been spotted is firmware version S948BXXU6ZZK3, and it's for the S26 Ultra only, though other S26 phones and servers will almost certainly get the beta. Enthusiast siteSammyGurualso expects the S25 series,Z Fold 8and Z Flip 8 to get the beta as well. Even if you have an S26, though, you may miss out if you bought it through a carrier. The One UI 8.5 beta was only available for unlocked phones in the US, and users with a carrier-locked S26 will probably have to wait for the stable release.
Samsung opened the One UI 8.5 beta on December 8, 2025, for the Galaxy S25, S25+ and S25 Ultra, but not everyone got it on day one: Owners in Poland and India had to wait until the second beta build on December 22. Samsung launched One UI 8.5 on the Galaxy S26 at its February 2026 Unpacked event, and released a beta for the Galaxy S24 series, Z Fold 6, Z Flip 6, S25 FE, S24 FE and Galaxy Tab S11 in late March.
The One UI 9.0 beta rolled out on May 13, and the stable version released with the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Z Flip 8 on July 22, in step with Google's Android 17 release. One UI 9.5 is still based on Android 17, putting it in the same mid-cycle slot 8.5 filled last year and timed for the next Galaxy S phones. As of writing, Samsung hasn't announced a date for the S27's Unpacked event, though it'll probably mirror recent years and fall somewhere in January or February.
Enthusiast siteSammyFanshas pencilled in early December for the beta, whileSamMobilethinks registrations could open in November. Both sites are working from a single previous point-five release, though; the S26's Ultra build sitting on Samsung's servers is a far better indication that a beta is imminent.
To sign up for the beta, you'll need a Samsung account and theSamsung Members app, which you can download from the Galaxy Store or Google Play. Once the beta itself goes live, you'll simply need to open Samsung Members, tap the One UI 9.5 banner or beta card on the home screen and select Registration for One UI Beta Program. If your phone and country qualify, Samsung will enrol you. From there, head toSettings>Software update>Download and installto get the beta. Samsung rolls builds out gradually, so don't panic if it doesn't show up immediately.
Before installing the beta, you should update all your apps and back up your phone to a computer with Smart Switch, since beta software can corrupt your data. If you come across any bugs, you can report them throughSamsung Members>Participated Beta test>Beta feedback>Send feedback.
Exiting the beta is the more awkward part. You can withdraw by navigating viaSamsung Members>Settings>Beta program settings>Withdraw from beta program, but that doesn't remove the beta build itself. Instead, you'll need to plug your phone into a computer and use Smart Switch to run a Downgrade, which will wipe everything you've done during testing. If you choose to stay on the beta, you'll get the finished One UI 9.5 as a normal update, whenever that is. So, if your S26 is your only phone and you don't keep regular backups, it's worth sitting this one out and waiting for the stable release.

Bomb threats have repeatedly affected flights across Europe this week, causing mass disruption.
Aer Lingus, Finnair, and Wizz Air said their aircraft had been cleared following security checks.
The incidents are being described as "hoax bomb threats" or "false attacks" by officials and airlines.

Flights across Europe were repeatedly targeted by "hoax" bomb threats this week, disrupting air travel across London, Copenhagen, Dublin, and Helsinki.
Danish police were investigating threats to air traffic at Copenhagen airport on Friday but did not find any immediate danger to passengers, according to reports from Reuters.
"We are once again at Copenhagen Airport today in connection with threats directed at air traffic," police said in a statement, per Reuters. "We are now investigating the incident and have a visible presence at the airport."
Meanwhile, Czech police also said Friday that there were threats to planes departing from and landing in Prague.
At least 27 different flights were impacted on Thursday, according toReuters, with some forced to land unexpectedly and others escorted by fighter jets.
Aer Lingus,Finnair, Wizz Air and Polish airline LOT confirmed to CNBC that some of their flights were affected.
It comes afterseven passenger planesacross Europe, two departing from the U.K., were targeted by suspected bomb threats on Tuesday and were described as "malicious hoax threats" by the U.K. government.
Finnair said two of its flights — one from Helsinki to Rome with 144 passengers and 7 crew members and another from Helsinki to Vienna with 177 passengers and six crew members — received "unfounded or hoax" bomb threats on Thursday, with both flights landing safely and customers disembarking the aircraft.
Local authorities in Rome and Vienna inspected the two flights and didn't find anything out of the ordinary.
"Unfortunately, air traffic is sometimes subject to threats, as we have seen this week, when other airlines in Europe have also faced hoax bomb threats," Finnair said in a statement. "Threats are almost always unfounded."
Hungarian budget carrier Wizz Air confirmed to CNBC that its flight from Milan's Malpensa Airport to Bucharest's Otopeni Airport, as well as another flight to Warsaw, were subject to bomb threats on Thursday.
The flight to Bucharest was approaching its final destination and landed safely when the threat was reported at Otopeni, with security checks subsequently clearing the aircraft. Wizz Air's Warsaw flight was diverted.
"This incident comes amid a series of similar bomb threats affecting several airlines across Europe in recent days," Wizz Air told CNBC. "Wizz Air is not the only airline targeted, with other carriers also experiencing threats resulting in flight diversions and security checks."
Irish airline Aer Lingus diverted its Dublin to Rome flight to Normandy on Thursday morning, while Polish airline LOT said two of its flights from Warsaw received security threats. Both were cleared following security inspections, the airlines told CNBC.
Separately, a French prosecutor opened an investigation into whether the pilot of an Aer Lingus plane refused to land in Evreux in northern France following a bomb threat prompting a diversion.
The pilot reportedly refused to comply with the French authorities' directions to land the plane, before being forced by two fighter jets to comply. Prosecutor Remi Coutin said he'll be probing whether the refusal to comply amounts to a criminal offense.
Air France's CEO Ben Smith said none of its flights were affected, but the coordinated threats are unprecedented. "It's unfortunate, and we hope it won't give consumers any reason to slow down or reduce their travel plans."
U.S. Transport Secretary Sean Duffy told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Thursday that the incidents appeared to be "false attacks."

European Union Commissioner for Sustainable Transport and Tourism,Apostolos Tzitzikostascautioned it is "too early to draw conclusions on whether the reported incidents are linked," in a post onX. "The EU-level information-sharing mechanism has been activated related to aviation security."

Share New Zealand braces for knife-edge election: What you need to know on social media
Add Al Jazeera on GoogleNew Zealand's Prime Minister and National Party leader Christopher Luxon campaigns in his Botany electorate, Auckland, New Zealand, October 26, 2026 [David Rowland/Reuters]ByAl Jazeera StaffandReutersPublished On 5 Nov 20265 Nov 2026
Days ahead of New Zealand’s election, polls show the governing centre-right National Party and the opposition centre-left Labour Party neck and neck, with neither on course to win enough seats to govern alone.
The outcome of the November 7 election could be decided by smaller parties under the country’s unique electoral system.
list 1 of 2New Zealand PM Christopher Luxon calls national election for November 7
list 2 of 2New Zealand deputy PM heckled day after saying colonisation good for Maori
New Zealand holds a general election every three years under a mixed-member proportional (MMP) system.
Voters cast two ballots: one for a candidate in their local electorate and one for a party.
Winning candidates in each of the country’s 71 electorates take their seats automatically. There are seven electorates reserved for Maori, New Zealand’s Indigenous people. Maori voters can choose to enrol on either the Maori electoral roll or the general roll.
The party vote decides how many seats each party gets overall. About 49 more seats are filled from party lists so that each party’s share of parliament matches its proportional share of the vote.
A party needs either 5 percent of the party vote, or one electorate win, to get a seat. In New Zealand’s 120-seat parliament, a majority usually means 61.
If a party wins more electorates than its share of the party vote entitles it to, it keeps them and extra seats are added to parliament. That happened in 2023, when Te Pati Maori won six of the seven Maori electorates, but had only 3.1 percent of the overall party vote.
Because seats in parliament closely track with the party vote, one party rarely wins a majority.
Every government since the MMP system was instituted in 1996 has been a coalition headed by Labour or National, except in 2020, when Labour under then-Prime Minister Jacinda Ardernwon bigand governed alone.
New Zealand Te Pati Maori co-leader Rawiri Waititi [File: Charlotte Graham-McLay]
Incumbent Prime Minister Christopher Luxon is seeking a second term.
A former Air New Zealand chief executive, he entered parliament in 2020 as the MP for the Auckland seat of Botany and became leader of the National Party a year later.
He led National back to power in 2023, promising better economic management and ending six years of Labour-led government. He now governs in a three-party coalition with New Zealand First and ACT.
But his leadership has come under pressure. He survived two attempted no-confidence votes by National MPs in April and August, the second orchestrated by his own defence minister at the time.
The challenges came as his popularity declined, with rising economic pressure and political tensions within the governing coalition.
Labour leader Chris Hipkins, 48, is bidding to return to the top job.
First elected to parliament in 2008, he became prime minister in January 2023 after his predecessor, Ardern, resigned.
Helost power in an electionthat October but stayed on to lead Labour in opposition.
Labour Party leader Chris Hipkins poses at his desk in Parliament in Wellington, New Zealand, September 9, 2026 [Hagen Hopkins/Reuters]
Most parties are campaigning on the economy, but their suggested remedies differ widely.
National is pledging to return the budget to surplus through fiscal discipline while expanding the national pension scheme.
Labour is focusing on the cost of living, promising cheaper healthcare and transport. It also plans to invest in jobs, housing and infrastructure, and to strengthen public services.
Smaller parties on both sides are taking aim at power companies and supermarkets. The right-wing populist New Zealand First party wants to break up major electricity companies and split one of the largest supermarket operators in two.
The Greens want a state-owned power company, a publicly owned supermarket chain and tougher rules against excessive grocery prices. They are also calling for a wealth tax and higher taxes on big companies and banks, while cutting income tax for most people.
Opportunity, a centrist party, wants a land value tax.
Immigration and voting rights are on the agenda too. ACT wants to deport serious offenders regardless of how long they have lived in New Zealand. New Zealand First is seeking to restrict voting to citizens. Currently, the right to vote also extends to legal residents who have lived in New Zealand for more than 12 months continuously.
New Zealand Green Party co-leader Chloe Swarbrick [File: Charlotte Graham-McLay/AP]
The real contest is between two rival blocs. National would need both its current coalition partners again, while Labour would depend on the Greens and possibly Opportunity.
Recent polls show no clear winner. A handful of seats either way could decide who governs.
That makes the 5 percent threshold for party participation in parliament crucial. If a smaller party narrowly misses it and also wins no electorate, its votes produce no seats, which could cost its bloc the majority.

Everything you need to know from the US midterm elections - BBC News
Watch: Key moments from the US midterm election results
ByJames FitzGeraldandNardine Saad,Reporting fromLos Angeles
Democrats have won both the US Senate and House of Representatives, taking control of Congress for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.
Projected results have provided the party with a number of things to celebrate - and rival Republicans somereasons to commiserate.
Here is everything you need to know about some of the big Democratic wins and somehistoric firsts.
Democrats toast victories in deep-red Trump country
Democrats have tallied up victories in states that werecomfortably wonby Trump two years ago in the presidential election.
With James Talarico winning a seat in the US Senate seatand Gina Hinojosa being elected state governor, Democrats scored two statewide victories in Texas - ending a string of defeats they have endured for almost two generations.
James Talarico, the new US senator in Texas, and Gina Hinojosa, the state's new governor, toast their successes
Talarico's supporters went beserk as the projected results arrived at an election-night party, wrote the BBC's Gary O'Donoghue. Attendees hugged, kissed and drank to a reality they dared not believe would come true.
Hinojosa became the first Latina to be elected governor of the state.
Among the other states where history was made by the Democrats were Kansas, where Adam Hamilton took a closely-fought Senate seat - giving the state its first Democratic senator for nearly a century.
LIVE UPDATES: All the latest developments
BOWEN: Trump's loss limits powers at home, but it will likely be different abroad

NEWSLETTER: Sign up for Anthony Zurcher's analysis in your inbox
Senior party figures who cheered the results included Hakeem Jeffries, the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, who is now poised to take over as the Speaker of the lower chamber of Congress.
"Today begins the great American comeback," he told a crowd of supporters.
If Jeffries' colleagues choose to keep him as the leader of their party's delegation in House, he will be the next Speaker, taking over from Republican Mike Johnson and becoming the first black person to fill that role.
Trump congratulates opposition and acknowledges Iran and fuel prices were issues
Trump spoke throughout the evening to a number of US media outlets, striking a conciliatory tone andconceding that the Democrats did a "good job".
He said he would accept the results and that he was looking forward to working with the opposition party - albeit he would still have the power, as president, to veto legislation that Democrats advance through Congress.
Trump distanced himself from some of the Republican candidates who contested the election, saying: "In some cases they didn't like the candidates, and in some cases those candidates were not my friend."
He acknowledged that the US-Israel war on Iran, which has impacted consumer prices in the US, had affected the vote. Trump argued that high fuel prices meant voters could not see how well his economy was doing "as much as they should have", adding: "The gasoline was caused by Iran."
Listen to Americast: Democrats make historic shift in US politics
El-Sayed wins US Senate race in Michigan after fellow Democrat turns on him
Abdul El-Sayed has become the first Muslim person elected to the US Senate - after claiming victory in Michigan in what was one of a handful of closely fought contests. His win means the seat stays in Democratic hands.
He defeated Republican opponent Mike Rogers, who received the surprise backing of El-Sayed's Democratic rival in the primary contest, Haley Stevens, who changed her endorsement at the eleventh hour.
The race was one of the bitterest of the midterms. Trump invoked 9/11 and even called El-Sayed a "jihadist" without citing any evidence, prompting a backlash and accusations of Islamophobia.
El-Sayed triumphed in one of the bitterest contests of the midterms
El-Sayed's supporters went wild when he took the stage to celebrate his claimed victory, wrote the BBC's Nada Tawfik. He said: "Up until right about now, you might have noticed I always say 'inshallah,' or 'God willing,' whenever the outcome of this race was mentioned."
He went on to say: "But today, tonight, we can turn that 'inshallah' into 'alhamdulillah'. For the right-wing ops, that just means 'praise be to God.'"
Republicans unable to win by distancing from Trump
The defeat of Susan Collins, who has served as the Republican senator for Maine for three decades, was one indicator of the scale of the Republican losses.
She was felled by Democratic candidate Troy Jackson, a logger who sought to point to his background to persuade blue-collar Mainers to vote for him.
In a statement reported by US media, Collins conceded defeat and said it had been the "honour of my life" to serve the state for 30 years.
The BBC's Helena Humphrey described a sombre atmosphere at Collins's watch party in the city of Maine - where the song Closing Time was played.
There was a sombre atmosphere at the watch party for Republican Susan Collins
Collins entered the race as one of the most vulnerable incumbent Republicans seeking re-election, and found that her tactic to distance herself from Trump did not work.
Ashley Hinson suffered the same fate in Iowa, losing that closely-fought Senate seat to Josh Turek. Hinson had slightly distanced herself from the president, urging him to end the war with Iran and breaking with him on easing beef tariffs, while at the same time defending Trump's broader tariff policies as important.
History made by new black governors, first openly gay male senator and first Gen Z congresswoman
Among the other firsts of the night were in Florida, whereRepublican Byron Donalds has become the state's first black governor, following a hearty endorsement from Trump.
Donalds, who will take over the job from Ron DeSantis, said his state was the "envy of the nation", and that he would work to make the state more affordable.
The result was one of the few high points of an otherwise difficult evening for the Republicans.

fact_units.text: Here’s What You Need to Know | WIREDSkip to main content
It’s 2016, andyou’re wandering around the neighborhood at dusk.
On the prowl, you’re swiping on a smartphone to catch that elusive Snorlax and grow your collection inPokémon Go.
You, alongside hundreds of millions of other players, are enjoying a mixed-reality game built around lovable characters.
What you don’t realize is that these scans of your environment will one day helprobotsnavigate obstacles and interact with objects.
Niantic, the creator ofPokémon Go, sold the game last year and pivoted hard into one of Silicon Valley’s buzziest AI topics right now: world models.
“We’re very much about reconstructing the real world,” says Brian McClendon,Niantic Spatial’schief technology officer.
He hopes to leverage its trove of world data to build replicas.
Unlike the text-based nature oflarge language models, world models use visual inputs and can generate digital environments that simulate physics.
Thissoftwareis poised to seep into everyday life, without you necessarily ever interacting directly with world models.
2027 could be a major year for the expansion of home robotics anddriverless cars, both of which are bolstered by advances in world models.
It’s time to better understand how these bots think.
“So with a language model, you have a sentence, and it will predict the next word in the sentence,” says Oliver Cameron, the CEO ofOdyssey, an AI lab focused on world models.
“With a world model, you give it a visual state of the world, an image, and it will then predict the next visual state of the world.” These 3D generations can be used as digital training grounds.
“They’re simulations, but they look and feel real,” he says.
McClendon sees these world models as helping robots practice without physical movement or being in intended environments.

He says someone could take photos of where the robot is intended to function, generate a 3D model, and then let the software run “millions of simulations” to train the robot on the space’s parameters.
It’s not justhumanoid robotsthat could use simulated practice; driverless cars also improve using world models.
Without a human behind the wheel, split-second software reactions are paramount.

“Importantly, a world model must be able to react to the actions that we take in the world, and so it must understand physics, cause and effect, and how other objects and people change their actions in response to our own,” says Jamie Shotton, chief scientist atWayve, which builds world models designed for cars.
Wayve’s generative world model is powered, in part, by dashcam footage.
The startup uses it to recreate hazardous roads and other unsafe conditions that would not be practical to test in real life.
Beyond physical applications, developers are also analyzing how world models could impact video games.
Since physics and 3D rendering are core to video games, major players likeTencentare investing in their own world models.
You can expect large AI companies, like Google, to keep boasting about their latest world-model improvements.

Investors are also throwing money at insurgent big names in computer science that are turning their attention to the technology.Yann LeCun, Meta’s former chief AI scientist, raisedover a billion dollarsrecently to fund his Advanced Machines Intelligence startup.
Additionally, famed Stanfordcomputer scientist Fei-Fei Lilaunched a startup in 2024 calledWorld Labs, whichAMDacquired this year for over $8 billion.
Even if you plan on avoiding autonomous cars and domestic bots altogether, world models are already warping the labor market behind the scenes.
To simulate our physical world, AI labs need real people to record it.
Earlier this year, I strapped aniPhone to my foreheadand recorded hours of videos in my apartment.
I recorded my hands folding laundry, washing dishes, and pouring Diet Coke, selling the video data through an app for a fairly measly payout.
As more companies attempt to build better world models, even more gig work may demand this kind of data collection.
Between chasing virtual monsters in 2016 and selling videos of my chores in 2026, these systems are ingesting more and more of my physical life.

Now I can’t stop picturing the digital ghost of some humanoid robot trapped inside a simulation of my bedroom, endlessly folding my boxers with its metallic claws—getting slightly better with every pass.

Nations Championship: Why Wales have a lot to prove despite Japan win - BBC Sport
Image source,Huw Evans Picture AgencyImage caption,
Wales have won their previous two internationals at the Principality Stadium
Wales rugby wins have been in short supply in recent years.
So you would think victory in the opening match of a new campaign might be welcomed. Maybe even celebrated.
But the28-21 win against Japanin the Nations Championship was unconvincing, underwhelming and a nervy struggle.
Head coach Steve Tandy admitted he expected better and captain Dewi Lake stated his teamhad let themselves down at timesagainst Eddie Jones’ Japan.
It might have been a fourth victory in 13 internationals for Tandy, but the patchy performance left a lot to be desired.
There are much tougher tests to come with New Zealand the visitors in Cardiff next Saturday and Australia in the Welsh capital the following weekend.
BBC Sport Wales analyses what went right and wrong for Wales as the Nations Championship resumed.
Nations Championship: Wales edge Japan but underwhelm - reaction
The shining light was wing Louis Rees-Zammit, who produced a stellar player-of-the-match display.
He set out his stall early on with an incisive break to lift the crowd and later scored his first try in eight internationals.
It was Rees-Zammit‘s most influential international display since his return to rugby from his brief foray with American football and the NFL.
The Bristol star had dabbled with a move to full-back last season, but is now back in his preferred wing position where he can cause the most havoc.
"There aren’t many athletes that can come back from a different sport and get back to playing international rugby like he did so quickly,” said Tandy.
"By his own admission, Zam wants more. He wants to be one of the best wings in the world, if not the best.
"He's got all the attributes to do that, and he's kicked on.”
When the hosts were struggling to break down the Japan defence, Rees-Zammit popped up with powerful bursts, producing five of Wales' 16 line-breaks, making 121 metres and beating 13 defenders.
“The best teams in the world have people that can break the game up, do something out of nothing,” said Tandy.
"He gone up a level and he deserved his man-of-the-match performance."
Aaron Wainwright has joined Leicester from Dragons
Wales fans were looking for a statement performance against Japan. A marker to put down as the World Cup looms in under a year.
They were not provided with that but did witness a victory, however scratchy.
So Wales woke up on a Sunday morning with a Test victory to mark. That has not happened often in recent times.
Some of these Wales players will still remember the record-breaking 18-Test losing sequence between 2023 and 2025. If Wales players can take any positives this weekend, it will be victory.
As Tandy said afterwards, it is always easier to debrief a bonus-point victory.
Among the disjointed team performance, there were notable impressive individual displays from the usual suspects.
Back-row duo Aaron Wainwright and Jac Morgan excelled in attack and defence, full-back Blair Murray was a constant attacking threat and wing Josh Adams popped up with two tries.
Centre Eddie James showed glimpses of his power game in a new-look midfield partnership with Max Llewellyn.
While the centre combination did not set the world alight, it warrants further opportunites.
Tandy will not be content with Wales spending long periods defending and only having 40% in territory and possession.
This was emphasised in the tackle count as the hosts made 227 compared to Japan's 115, with Wales finishing with the top eight tacklers in the game.
He will be encouraged by the resolve with Morgan topping the official Nations Championship charts with 24, followed by lock Dafydd Jenkins (23) and Wainwright (20).
Wales also forced 10 turnovers with Alex Mann gaining three, while there were crucial interventions from Lake, Adams and prop Nicky Smith when Japan seemed destined to score.
Win is massive for confidence - Lake
The most obvious deficiency was the malfunctioning line-out with six throws going astray.
Hookers, Lake and Ryan Elias, struggled to find their jumpers as the Japan man mountain locks of Harry Hockings and co-captain Warner Dearns caused chaos.
Wales coughed up possession, but the line-out failures also disrupted the home side’s attacking maul, which has become the most potent offensive threat in recent time.
“We have got to be better,” said Lake.
“When we did get it right, we got joy from that area, but we would have loved to go to our driving maul more often.
“You have to credit Japan in that area for the defensive work they do.
"They're number one in the world for a reason in this department, but we're always going to look at ourselves first.”
Wales need to shed slow starter tags
Wales have been notoriously slow starters to new campaigns with Tandy’s team suffering heavy defeats by Argentina 12 months ago and England during the Six Nations in February.
This weekend has proved no exception against a side, like the southern hemisphere outfits, who are battle hardened.
“It's great for us to get a game,” said Tandy.
"It does get clunky in your first hit out since the summer.
"It takes time to build that cohesion back, whereas you look at the amount of games South Africa, New Zealand and Japan have played since the last time we did in July.
"If you look at last year's Six Nations, we got better in every game and we will look to do that again."
After threatening to take control, Wales continually let Japan back into the game as they were guilty of poor handling errors, bouts of indiscipline and lapses in concentration.
“There were moments where we'd go seven points up and there'd be a sloppy knock-on or we'd look for the pass from a line break rather than take the tackle,” said Tandy.
“There are bits where there's lots to like, but in Test matches, you need to be ruthless and reward yourself when on top.”
Wales fly-half Sam Costelow also had a mixed evening as he was guilty of kicking attacking ball away when the home side seemed set to break down the Japan defence.
Neither Costelow or Dan Edwards have nailed down the famous Wales number 10 jersey. The debate about who should fill the shirt will continue.
Wales remain 10th in the world with this victory again coming against a nation ranked between ninth and 12th.
